q: A retailer needs to predict next week’s revenue in rand for each store using historical sales and promotions. Managers will later label each prediction as above or below target. Which technique should produce the revenue estimate?
options: Regression on historical sales and promotions
why: Regression predicts the numeric revenue amount. The later above/below-target label is a separate calculation using that prediction.

clues.why: The model must estimate an amount, not a group or label.

hint: Identify the output required before the manager applies the target rule.
analysis: Separate the prediction from the later report. Revenue in rand is a numeric target; a threshold label does not turn the underlying amount prediction into classification.
trap: Choosing a technique for the downstream label instead of the requested prediction.
reasons: Classification predicts a category or band, rather than the requested revenue amount.
Regression learns a relationship between input features and a numeric target such as revenue.
Clustering groups similar stores without directly learning the requested revenue target.
Anomaly detection identifies unusual observations rather than predicting the expected revenue amount.
transfer: Predicting a lease payment amount is regression; predicting whether a lease will default is classification.

q: A model learns from emails already marked spam or safe. What is this?
why: Supervised learning uses labeled examples. The spam labels supply the target answers.

clues.why: Known target labels are available during training.

hint: Ask whether the desired answers are supplied with the examples.
analysis: The key condition is that training emails already have spam/safe labels. That is different from discovering groups without labels.
trap: Spam is the application; labeled examples determine the learning type.
reasons: Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels.
Reinforcement learning uses feedback about actions and rewards, not just labeled email examples.
Supervised learning maps examples to known target labels.
Pre-training describes a training stage, not the best description of these labeled examples.

q: Which metric matters most when missing actual fraud is especially costly?
why: Recall measures the proportion of actual fraud cases detected, directly addressing missed positives.

clues.why: False negatives are the error the business most wants to reduce.

hint: Focus on the costliest error, not a generic overall score.
analysis: Find the priority: catching actual fraud. Recall measures detected positives out of all actual positives.
trap: High accuracy can hide missed fraud when most transactions are legitimate.
reasons: Recall measures the proportion of actual fraud cases detected, directly addressing missed positives.
Precision measures how trustworthy positive fraud alerts are, rather than how many actual fraud cases were missed.
Accuracy can be dominated by legitimate transactions when fraud is rare.
F1 balances precision and recall; the stated priority specifically emphasizes missed fraud and therefore recall.

q: Which AWS service converts recorded speech into text?
why: Transcribe recognizes speech. Polly does the reverse: text to speech.

clues.why: Check the direction of conversion.

hint: Identify what goes in and what must come out.
analysis: Audio is the input and a transcript is the output. Choose speech recognition rather than speech synthesis.
trap: Polly and Transcribe are easy to reverse: read the input/output direction.
reasons: Polly generates speech from text, the reverse direction.
Translate converts text between languages.
Comprehend analyzes text; it does not transcribe audio.
Transcribe converts speech recordings into text.

q: Which TWO tasks should primarily use deterministic rules rather than a probabilistic model?
options: Group customers by similar purchasing behavior
Calculate a tax amount using an exact published formula
Enforce whether an identity has permission to read a restricted object
reasons: Grouping by similarity can use ML clustering.
An exact formula should be computed directly rather than estimated.
Object recognition is a common computer-vision task.
Authorization must be enforced by a policy decision, not guessed by a model.
Forecasting unknown future values is a common prediction task.
why: Exact formulas and permission enforcement require rule-based outcomes, while clustering, vision and forecasting can benefit from learned predictions.

clues.why: Choose tasks requiring exact calculation or an enforced access decision.

hint: Look for exact outcomes, and select exactly two tasks.
analysis: Distinguish uncertain prediction from actions that must follow exact rules. Both the calculation and the authorization condition need deterministic enforcement.
trap: A model may help describe a rule, but it should not replace the calculation or authorization control.

q: A team uses a model priced per input token. Two prompts ask the same question with different wording. Their word counts are equal, but their quoted input costs differ. Which measurement best explains the difference?
options: The number of user requests submitted
The number of complete words supplied
The number of tokens produced by the model’s tokenizer
The number of characters displayed to the user
why: Token-based input pricing uses the token count for the selected model. Equal word counts do not guarantee equal token counts.

clues.why: The measurement must match the stated pricing unit.

hint: Use the provider’s stated billing unit rather than a convenient text-length estimate.
analysis: The scenario specifies input-token pricing. Compare tokenized inputs using the same model and price; total inference cost can also include output tokens.
trap: Treating one word as exactly one token, or confusing input cost with the total bill.
reasons: Both prompts are single requests; request count does not explain different input-token charges.
A word may be represented by one or several tokens, so equal word counts can have different costs.
The tokenizer determines the model’s input units, which are used for the stated pricing model.
Character counts can be a rough proxy but are not the billing unit in this scenario.
transfer: Changing languages or including code can change token counts even when the request means the same thing.

q: What does an embedding represent?
options: An encrypted copy of the source text
A numeric representation of semantic features
The position of a word in a billing record
A confidence score proving an answer is factual
why: Embeddings encode features in numeric vectors used in tasks such as semantic similarity search.

clues.why: The concept represents semantic information numerically.

hint: Look for a representation that enables similarity comparison.
analysis: Identify what embeddings do: encode features in vectors, allowing related content to be compared.
trap: A vector is a representation, not encryption or a guarantee of meaning.
reasons: Embeddings are representations, not encryption, and should not be treated as protection against data disclosure.
Embeddings encode features in numeric vectors used in tasks such as semantic similarity search.
A billing-record position does not describe semantic vector representation.
A vector embedding does not prove an answer is correct or supply a calibrated factual confidence score.

q: A chatbot invents a believable citation. What is this called?
why: Fabricating a plausible citation is an example of hallucination: generated content without factual support.

clues.why: The output sounds credible but lacks factual support.

hint: Distinguish fluent wording from verified evidence.
analysis: The failure is fabricated factual content. Neither a confident tone nor a citation-shaped string proves truth.
trap: Do not treat a plausible citation as a checked source.
reasons: Data poisoning corrupts training or source data; the scenario describes an unsupported generated assertion.
Prompt injection involves instructions trying to redirect the system; no such attack is described.
Fabricating a plausible citation is an example of hallucination: generated content without factual support.
Distillation trains a smaller model from a teacher and is not the name for fabricated content.

q: Which service offers managed access to foundation models from multiple providers?
why: Bedrock provides managed foundation-model access. S3 stores objects; Config tracks resource configuration.

clues.why: The requirement is managed foundation-model access, not storage.

hint: Choose the service whose main purpose matches the requested capability.
analysis: Match both conditions: managed model access and a choice of providers. Other cloud services may support the application but do not provide this capability.
trap: A component used by an AI app is not necessarily the model-access service.
reasons: CloudTrail provides activity logging for audit use.
S3 stores objects; it does not itself provide managed model inference.
Config tracks resource configuration and compliance rules.
Bedrock offers managed access to foundation models from different providers.

q: An internal assistant must connect to tools, respect access limits, use changing policies and adopt a response style. Match each requirement to the most direct concept. Use each option once.
reasons: IAM policies control permitted actions on AWS resources; a tool connection does not grant those permissions.
Fine-tuning adapts weights using training examples; it is different from inserting documents into a prompt.
MCP standardizes connections to external tools and context; authorization is still needed.
RAG retrieves relevant source material for the current request without retraining the foundation model.
why: MCP connects tools, IAM authorizes access, RAG supplies retrieved context and fine-tuning adapts model weights. These capabilities can complement one another.

clues.why: Match each responsibility rather than choosing an entire architecture.

hint: Distinguish connection, permission, runtime information and training.
analysis: Match the verb in each requirement to the capability. An application may use all four, but each requirement asks for one primary role.
trap: Assuming that connecting a tool authorizes it, or that retrieving a document trains the model.
prompts: Standardize discovery and calls to supported external tools
Decide which AWS resources its identity may access
Supply current policy passages at request time
Adapt model weights using approved response examples
transfer: A connected expense tool still needs access checks; retrieving its latest policy does not change the model’s weights.

q: An employee assistant must answer from a large policy library that changes daily and show supporting passages. The team will keep its existing foundation model. Which design best meets both requirements?
options: Retrieve relevant passages from a synchronized policy index and attach source references
Fine-tune weekly on the policies and ask the model to name its sources
Cache generated policy answers and refresh them after users report changes
Add a link to the policy website in the system prompt without retrieving its content
why: RAG can supply current, relevant policy passages and their source references at answer time. The source-to-index synchronization must also stay current.

clues.why: The information pipeline must reflect updates.
The answer needs retrieved evidence, not just a source name.

hint: Check how each approach obtains updated evidence and makes it traceable.
analysis: Both daily changes and supporting passages matter. Choose current retrieval with source metadata, then check that answers are supported by the retrieved text.
trap: Assuming that a generated citation or a current-looking URL proves the answer is grounded.
reasons: Retrieval from an updated index supplies both current evidence and traceable passages.
Weekly training can lag daily changes, and naming a source is not evidence that its passage was retrieved.
Cached answers can remain stale until a user notices; they do not meet the requirement for current supporting passages.
A URL alone does not give the model access to the page or retrieve supporting text.
transfer: For a changing product catalogue, refresh retrieval data and check grounding; retraining alone does not supply current source passages.

q: A prompt includes three examples of the desired response. Which technique is used?
why: Few-shot prompting supplies examples in context. It does not update model weights.

clues.why: The prompt demonstrates the desired behavior.

hint: Count examples in the prompt, not model parameters.
analysis: Three demonstrations supplied in the prompt make this few-shot prompting. The model is not being trained on a new dataset.
trap: Examples in a prompt are not automatically fine-tuning.
reasons: Zero-shot prompting does not supply task demonstrations.
Distillation trains a student to learn from a teacher model.
Few-shot prompting uses a small number of examples in context.
Pre-training learns model parameters from a broad training corpus.

q: Repeated runs of the same summarization prompt produce too much variation. The model exposes temperature and a maximum-output-token setting. The team wants less sampling randomness while retaining room for a complete summary. Which change best fits?
options: Lower temperature while keeping the output-token budget unchanged
Lower the output-token budget while keeping temperature unchanged
Add stop sequences while keeping temperature unchanged
Cache the first summary and reuse it for every later document
why: Lower temperature generally favors higher-probability next tokens, reducing sampling variation without directly shortening the output allowance.

clues.why: The requested behavior is controlled by a sampling parameter.

hint: Distinguish a sampling control from a length control or response reuse.
analysis: The requested change concerns variability, with output space preserved. Evaluate lower temperature on representative summaries and check factual accuracy separately.
trap: Assuming less randomness guarantees truth, or reducing length when the problem is variability.
reasons: This adjusts sampling randomness while preserving room for the summary; it does not guarantee identical or factual responses.
The token budget limits length and may truncate a summary, rather than directly controlling sampling randomness.
Stop sequences terminate generation at specified text; they do not directly adjust the sampling distribution.
Reusing one answer for different documents can return the wrong summary and does not tune generation.
transfer: For repeated extraction tasks, lower temperature may improve consistency, but schema validation and factual checks remain necessary.

q: A team wants a smaller model to learn from a larger model’s outputs. What is this?
why: Distillation trains a smaller student to learn from a larger teacher model.

clues.why: A smaller student is learning from a larger teacher.

hint: Distinguish training a student from retrieving documents.
analysis: The goal is transferring capabilities from a larger model to a smaller one. That is a model-training relationship rather than context retrieval.
trap: Do not confuse distillation with compressing a prompt.
reasons: Few-shot prompting supplies examples at inference time without training a student model.
RAG retrieves source material for context and does not itself train a student.
Prompt caching reuses supported processing of repeated context rather than transferring model capabilities.
Distillation trains a smaller student to learn from a larger teacher model.

q: Which outcome best measures a support agent’s business usefulness?
why: Measure task completion against cost and quality goals, rather than model size alone.

clues.why: The measure must reflect a real user outcome.

hint: Ask what success means to the business.
analysis: The task is evaluating a support agent as a product. Successful task completion balanced with cost and quality is more meaningful than size or verbosity.
trap: A larger model or longer answer is not automatically more useful.
reasons: Task completion with acceptable cost connects performance to a business objective.
Long answers may be irrelevant or costly; length alone is not success.
Parameter count is a model characteristic, not a direct business result.
Vector count indicates stored representations, not customer outcomes.

q: A hiring model has high overall accuracy. One demographic group reports more mistaken rejections, but few members of that group appear in the evaluation data. What is the best first investigation?
options: Compare average model confidence across all applicants
Compare subgroup false-rejection rates and whether each sample supports a reliable conclusion
Remove demographic labels from the evaluation data and repeat the aggregate score
Apply the same decision threshold to every group and report the original accuracy
why: Subgroup error rates investigate the reported harm, while sample adequacy determines how confidently those rates can be compared.

clues.why: Investigate the relevant error, not confidence alone.
A small sample can make comparisons unreliable.

hint: Measure the reported harm for the affected group, then check the strength of the evidence.
analysis: A high average does not answer a subgroup question. Investigate error rates and representation before selecting a mitigation; handle demographic data with suitable privacy controls.
trap: Treating equal thresholds, confidence or aggregate accuracy as proof of fairness.
reasons: Overall confidence can conceal subgroup errors and is not a measure of the reported false rejections.
This directly investigates the reported error and the strength of the supporting evidence.
Removing labels prevents the proposed subgroup comparison; it does not establish fairness.
A common threshold alone does not establish comparable error rates or fix an inadequate evaluation sample.
transfer: A service can score well overall while working poorly for a language or region with little evaluation data.

q: What does model explainability help users understand?
options: How to reduce endpoint hosting costs
How to encrypt every training record
Whether every prediction is guaranteed factual
why: Explainability helps people interpret influential factors or reasons behind a model prediction.

clues.why: The user needs an interpretation of the model’s decision.

hint: Separate explanation from access to raw training data.
analysis: The goal is understanding the reasons or influential factors behind a prediction. This does not require exposing confidential training records.
trap: An explanation of influential factors is not a proof of causation.
reasons: Hosting-cost optimization is an operational concern, not what explainability describes.
Explainability helps people interpret influential factors or reasons behind a model prediction.
Encryption protects data; it does not explain a particular prediction.
An explanation is not a guarantee that a prediction is correct or fair.

q: Which feature helps filter harmful content in a Bedrock application?
why: Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content safeguards, which should be evaluated alongside other controls.

clues.why: The required capability is a generation safeguard.

hint: Choose a control that acts on model input or output.
analysis: Match a content-safety requirement to a configurable safeguard. Keep other controls and evaluation because filtering is imperfect.
trap: Guardrails reduce risk; they are not an absolute safety guarantee.
reasons: Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content safeguards, which should be evaluated alongside other controls.
IAM controls authorization; it does not itself classify and filter generated harmful text.
CloudTrail supports auditing account activity rather than directly filtering a response.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it is not the Bedrock response content-filter feature.

q: What should a team assess before commercial use of generated artwork?
why: Generated content can carry intellectual-property risks. Review rights and intended use before publishing.

clues.why: The intended use raises rights and licensing questions.

hint: Ask what nontechnical risk remains even when generation succeeds.
analysis: The scenario asks what to assess before publication, not how to improve model performance. Rights and intellectual-property risks directly affect commercial reuse.
trap: Being generated by AI does not automatically grant unrestricted rights.
reasons: Dimensions affect presentation, not permission to use the artwork.
Rendering speed affects efficiency, not licensing or ownership risk.
Token count is not evidence of intellectual-property clearance.
Usage rights and IP risks should be assessed for the intended use.

q: Which approach best supports safe, high-impact AI decisions?
options: Automatically approve outputs above a confidence threshold
Expose technical confidence scores without a review process
Use human review and a process to correct harmful errors
Assume a large model makes oversight unnecessary
why: Human oversight and correction mechanisms help detect and address harmful errors in high-impact decisions.

clues.why: Errors could seriously affect people.

hint: Choose safeguards proportional to the consequence of a mistake.
analysis: High-impact use calls for meaningful oversight and correction mechanisms. Automation alone cannot justify approving every output.
trap: A confident model can still make a harmful decision.
reasons: A confidence threshold alone does not provide adequate review for every high-impact use.
Scores alone do not create a meaningful path to review or correction.
Human oversight and correction mechanisms help detect and address harmful errors in high-impact decisions.
Model scale does not remove error, bias or accountability concerns.

q: An AI application should access only its required S3 objects. Apply which principle?
options: Make the bucket publicly readable for easier access
Encrypt the bucket but grant broad read permissions
Give the application a shared administrator credential
why: Least privilege restricts permitted actions and resources to those required for the application.

clues.why: Scope access to the actual task.

hint: Look for the smallest sufficient permission boundary.
analysis: The application needs specific objects, so permissions should be limited to those resources and necessary actions.
trap: An application needing access does not justify broad account permissions.
reasons: Public access exceeds the application’s need and may expose objects to others.
Least privilege restricts permitted actions and resources to those required for the application.
Encryption protects data but does not justify giving an application excess authorization.
Administrator credentials exceed the required scope and weaken accountability when shared.

q: Which AWS service records account API activity for auditing?
why: CloudTrail records supported account API events and related activity for audit and investigation.

clues.why: The requirement is an audit trail of account actions.

hint: Distinguish API auditing from model inference and text services.
analysis: The investigator needs records of supported account API events. Select the auditing service rather than language-processing capabilities.
trap: Logs serve different purposes; account activity is distinct from text generation.
reasons: Operational metrics are not a substitute for an account API activity audit trail.
Config tracks resource configuration; it does not replace the requested API event history.
CloudTrail records supported account API events and related activity for audit and investigation.
Artifact provides compliance documents rather than recording your account’s API calls.

q: Which service helps discover sensitive data in Amazon S3?
why: Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3 objects.

clues.why: The goal is identifying sensitive content in stored objects.

hint: Separate discovery of sensitive data from encryption of that data.
analysis: The combination of data discovery and S3 points to a purpose-built sensitive-data service. Discovery does not itself solve every protection requirement.
trap: Finding sensitive data is different from controlling who may read it.
reasons: Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3 objects.
KMS manages cryptographic keys; it does not perform the requested sensitive-content discovery.
CloudTrail records account activity, not a content classification scan of S3 objects.
IAM controls access permissions rather than discovering sensitive content.

q: A retrieved document tells an agent to reveal secrets. What is the main threat?
why: Prompt injection attempts to redirect an AI system through untrusted instructions, such as retrieved text.

clues.why: The instructions are arriving through untrusted source content.

hint: Ask whether source data is being promoted into authority.
analysis: A document is attempting to redirect the agent and expose secrets. Treat retrieved content as data and keep tool permissions outside its control.
trap: RAG grounding does not make retrieved instructions trustworthy.
reasons: The document is issuing hostile instructions rather than merely causing an unsupported factual statement.
Underfitting concerns inadequate learning and does not describe this instruction attack.
An output-length cap concerns generation size, not a request to reveal secrets.
Prompt injection attempts to redirect an AI system through untrusted instructions, such as retrieved text.

q: Which practice makes a training dataset’s origins traceable?
options: Store a model accuracy score without dataset metadata
Retain only the current dataset filename
Record the endpoint latency for each request
why: Lineage documents where the data came from and how it changed.

clues.why: The goal is documenting provenance and transformations.

hint: Look for the practice that lets an auditor follow the data’s history.
analysis: Traceability requires recording where data came from and how it changed. Access credentials do not provide that history.
trap: Logging everything without recording provenance may still leave the origin unclear.
reasons: Accuracy alone does not identify data origins or transformations.
Lineage documents where the data came from and how it changed.
A filename alone usually does not provide the full provenance or transformation history.
Latency measures response time, not dataset provenance.

q: A retailer groups customers by similar purchasing behavior without predefined segment labels. Which technique fits?
why: Clustering discovers groups based on similarity without predefined target labels.
reasons: Regression predicts a numeric target, not unlabeled groups.
Clustering discovers groups based on similarity without predefined target labels.
Binary classification needs a defined two-class target rather than unknown segments.
Speech recognition transcribes audio and is unrelated to this grouping task.

clues.why: The groups are not known targets.

hint: Decide whether labels are given or groups must be discovered.
analysis: The desired output is customer groups, and no labels exist. This combines a grouping goal with unsupervised learning.
trap: Unlabeled does not automatically mean clustering; the grouping objective is also essential.

q: A spam filter raises false alarms on legitimate emails. Which metric directly asks how many predicted spam emails really are spam?
why: Precision measures actual positives among predicted positives, matching alert reliability.
reasons: Recall asks how many actual spam messages were found, not whether spam alerts are trustworthy.
Accuracy mixes correct spam and safe predictions and may hide the relevant error.
Precision measures actual positives among predicted positives, matching alert reliability.
Mean absolute error measures numeric prediction error, not class-alert reliability.

clues.why: The denominator is the set of positive predictions.

hint: Write out which group appears after the phrase out of.
analysis: The question conditions on emails predicted as spam. Precision evaluates the correctness of that positive-prediction group.
trap: Precision and recall differ in their denominator, even when both discuss correct positives.

q: A classifier achieves excellent training results but performs poorly on unseen examples. What is the most likely issue?
why: Strong training results with poor unseen performance suggest fitting training-specific patterns that do not generalize.
reasons: Underfitting generally produces inadequate performance even on the training data.
Strong training results with poor unseen performance suggest fitting training-specific patterns that do not generalize.
Expected generalization would produce adequate results on unseen examples too.
Latency is response time and does not explain the described training-versus-test quality gap.

clues.why: Generalization, not training memorization, is the concern.

hint: Compare training performance with performance on new data.
analysis: A large training-versus-unseen performance gap suggests overfitting. Diagnose the gap rather than celebrating the training score.
trap: More training accuracy alone can worsen the actual problem.

q: A team has defined a churn-prediction goal and collected historical records. Order the remaining stages so the final test data does not influence model selection. Use each stage once.
options: Train candidates and select settings using the training and validation sets
Deploy the accepted model and monitor real-world outcomes
Prepare suitable training, validation and untouched test sets
Evaluate the selected model on the untouched test set against acceptance criteria
reasons: Training fits candidates; validation supports model selection without using final test results.
Deployment follows an acceptable evaluation, and monitoring checks real-world behavior.
Establish the splits before fitting; learn preprocessing parameters from training data and apply them to held-out data.
Use the untouched test set for final assessment after model selection, rather than repeatedly tuning to its results.
why: Separate the data first, train and select using development data, evaluate on the untouched test set, then deploy only if acceptance criteria are met.

clues.text: final test data does not influence model selection
clues.why: Keep the test set separate from training and validation.

hint: Identify when data must be reserved and which evidence should support the release decision.
analysis: The split must precede fitting and model selection. Test results should support a release decision rather than become another tuning signal; monitor after deployment.
trap: Selecting settings using the final test set, which makes the reported final assessment overly optimistic.
transfer: If you repeatedly change a prompt after reading its test results, reserve a fresh assessment set before claiming general performance.

q: A website needs a prediction while a customer is waiting at checkout. Which inference pattern fits best?
why: Real-time inference serves low-latency predictions for interactive requests.
reasons: Nightly batch processing does not return a result during the current checkout.
Real-time inference serves low-latency predictions for interactive requests.
Training creates or updates the model; it is not the live prediction step.
Labeling prepares examples rather than responding to the customer.

clues.why: The result is needed during an interactive transaction.

hint: Identify the required response time before selecting a processing pattern.
analysis: The checkout request needs an immediate prediction. Real-time inference matches this latency condition.
trap: A prediction workload is not necessarily a training workload.

q: A team processes millions of records overnight and does not need immediate responses. Which inference pattern is most appropriate?
why: Batch inference suits large groups of predictions without an immediate-response requirement.
reasons: Interactive endpoints can work but do not best match the stated overnight bulk requirement.
Labeling is a data-preparation task, not inference over the records.
Batch inference suits large groups of predictions without an immediate-response requirement.
Retraining for each record confuses model training with using a trained model.

clues.why: Bulk processing can be deferred.

hint: Look for whether results are required immediately or can arrive together later.
analysis: The workload is large and delay is acceptable. A bulk prediction pattern fits better than a per-user interactive pattern.
trap: Large volume alone is not enough; the relaxed latency requirement matters too.

q: A mobile app must read a prepared text message aloud. Which AWS service fits?
why: Polly generates speech from text.
reasons: Transcribe turns speech into text, the reverse direction.
Comprehend analyzes text, such as sentiment or entities.
Translate converts languages but does not supply the requested speech output.
Polly generates speech from text.

clues.why: Text is the input; audio is the output.

hint: State the input and output formats before looking at the service names.
analysis: The task is text-to-speech synthesis. No transcription or language conversion is requested.
trap: Do not choose a speech-related service without checking the conversion direction.

q: A game-playing model learns by taking actions and receiving rewards. Which learning approach fits?
options: Supervised learning from fixed class labels
why: Reinforcement learning optimizes behavior based on interaction and rewards.
reasons: Fixed labeled examples differ from learning through actions and reward signals.
Reinforcement learning optimizes behavior based on interaction and rewards.
Clustering discovers groups rather than a rewarded action policy.
Regression predicts numbers; it does not describe the action-and-reward learning setup.

clues.why: The feedback evaluates actions in an environment.

hint: Ask how the learning system receives feedback.
analysis: Actions, environment feedback and rewards characterize reinforcement learning. The fact that it is a game is only supporting context.
trap: Not every game AI uses reinforcement learning; the described feedback mechanism determines the answer.

q: A company needs one model to interpret a product photo and answer a text question about it. Which capability is required?
why: The model must understand both visual content and text to answer the request.
reasons: A text-only model cannot directly interpret the product image.
The model must understand both visual content and text to answer the request.
Text embeddings alone do not provide the requested image interpretation and response.
Speech transcription handles audio, not the product photo.

clues.text: photo and answer a text question
clues.why: Two input/output modalities are involved.

hint: List the content formats that the model must handle.
analysis: The required capability spans image interpretation and language. Select support for both modalities.
trap: A model that generates images is not necessarily a model that understands image inputs.

q: An on-demand model charges per input and output token. Which change most directly reduces generation cost when answer quality remains acceptable?
options: Increase the maximum output for every request
Send all conversation history whether relevant or not
Remove unnecessary prompt text and cap output while checking quality
Fine-tune a larger model solely to increase its parameter count
why: For the stated token-priced model, reducing unnecessary input and output can lower cost while preserving the required quality.
reasons: A larger output allowance can increase token usage instead of reducing it.
Irrelevant history increases billed input without necessarily helping answer quality.
For the stated token-priced model, reducing unnecessary input and output can lower cost while preserving the required quality.
Increasing model size is not a direct remedy for excessive token use and may add costs.

clues.why: Both sides of the interaction can affect billing.

hint: Match the cost driver to the resource you can reduce.
analysis: This question explicitly states a token-based price. Trim irrelevant input and unnecessary output, then verify the answer still satisfies the task.
trap: The shortest answer is not automatically best if it loses necessary information.

q: A team wants a general-purpose model already trained on broad datasets to adapt to several tasks. What type of model is this?
why: A foundation model is broadly trained and can support multiple downstream tasks.
reasons: A foundation model is broadly trained and can support multiple downstream tasks.
A fixed business rule is not a broadly trained adaptable model.
A database index speeds retrieval; it is not a generative model.
An access policy governs authorization rather than learning tasks.

clues.why: Broad pre-training supports adaptation across tasks.

hint: Separate a reusable learned model from a fixed rule or infrastructure component.
analysis: The defining property is broad training followed by reuse across tasks. A task-specific classifier alone would not imply this scope.
trap: General-purpose does not mean accurate for every business task without evaluation.

q: Order these stages in a simplified foundation-model lifecycle, including optional adaptation.
options: Evaluate the adapted model against task requirements
Deploy the model and collect feedback
Select and curate suitable training data
Adapt the model if the target task needs it
reasons: Evaluate the result of training/adaptation before deployment.
Pre-training requires selected and prepared data.
Deployment follows evaluation; feedback can inform later iterations.
Data selection and curation support the subsequent training stage.
Task adaptation follows a base model and is not always necessary.
why: Curate data → pre-train → adapt if needed → evaluate → deploy and collect feedback.

clues.why: Place adaptation after a base model exists and before its final task evaluation.

hint: Trace the dependencies from source data to a deployed model.
analysis: The simplified sequence starts with data, produces a base model, optionally adapts it, evaluates suitability, then deploys with feedback.
trap: The ordered exercise is a simplified dependency chain; real projects can iterate and evaluate at multiple points.

q: An assistant selects a tool, checks its result and chooses a next action toward a goal. What is the key capability?
why: An agent can select and use tools as part of a goal-directed workflow.
reasons: Storage holds data and does not choose goal-directed actions.
An agent can select and use tools as part of a goal-directed workflow.
Tokenization prepares text units but does not describe planning and actions.
A fixed lookup alone does not describe selecting and iterating on tool actions.

clues.why: The system is taking goal-directed actions, beyond generating text.

hint: Look for decisions and tool use rather than conversational tone.
analysis: The assistant uses observations to guide further actions. That is the agentic part of the description.
trap: A chatbot is not automatically an agent just because it sounds conversational.

q: A company can call a suitable foundation model through a managed API instead of hosting its own model servers. What is a likely advantage?
why: A managed API reduces the infrastructure the customer must operate directly.
reasons: Application owners still need to evaluate output quality and suitability.
A managed API reduces the infrastructure the customer must operate directly.
Customers retain responsibilities such as permissions and appropriate data handling.
Managed inference can still incur usage charges.

clues.text: instead of hosting its own model servers
clues.why: The comparison concerns operating the infrastructure.

hint: Choose an operational benefit without turning it into an absolute guarantee.
analysis: The benefit is reduced server operations. Managed service does not remove evaluation, cost or all customer responsibilities.
trap: Beware options claiming a managed service eliminates every responsibility.

q: An app prepares relevant documents, conversation history and tool descriptions for a model call. Which concept best describes this?
why: Context engineering organizes useful information and instructions supplied to a model at runtime.
reasons: Context engineering organizes useful information and instructions supplied to a model at runtime.
Runtime context preparation does not itself update model weights.
Encryption protects data; it does not choose relevant context for a call.
Class-label balancing concerns training-data distribution rather than runtime context.

clues.why: The information is being assembled at inference time.

hint: Distinguish changing the input from changing the trained model.
analysis: Relevant context and tool information are prepared before inference. This is a runtime design task, not necessarily training.
trap: A long prompt is not automatically well-engineered context.

q: A product needs an open-source framework for building model-driven agents on AWS. Which option is designed for agent development?
why: Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for building model-driven agents.
reasons: Artifact provides access to compliance documents and agreements.
Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3.
Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for building model-driven agents.
Config tracks resource configuration and rule compliance.

clues.why: The requirement is development tooling for agents.

hint: Match the requested development role, not simply a service that mentions AI security.
analysis: An agent-building SDK fits the development requirement. Compliance and data-discovery tools support other concerns.
trap: Services in the same ecosystem do not all perform the same job.

q: A team wants managed runtime and supporting services for operating agents at scale. Which AWS offering is designed for this?
why: Bedrock AgentCore provides services for deploying and operating agents.
reasons: Polly synthesizes speech rather than operating general-purpose agent workloads.
Bedrock AgentCore provides services for deploying and operating agents.
Artifact provides compliance documents, not an agent runtime.
Translate converts text between languages rather than hosting agents.

clues.why: The requirement is operational support, not only writing agent code.

hint: Distinguish an agent-development framework from managed runtime services.
analysis: Focus on deployment and operations for agents. AgentCore is designed for that role, whereas specialized language services are not a general runtime.
trap: Writing an agent and operating it reliably are different requirements.

q: A company wants an assistant that helps develop software from specifications. Which AWS tool best fits?
why: Kiro is an AI development tool supporting specification-driven software development.
reasons: Transcribe converts speech recordings to text.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.
Polly converts text into speech.
Kiro is an AI development tool supporting specification-driven software development.

clues.why: The application is software development, not speech processing.

hint: Identify the business workflow before selecting the tool.
analysis: The request concerns moving specifications into software development work. Choose the development tool rather than a specialized text/audio service.
trap: AI-related names alone do not establish a match to the workflow.

q: Two models meet quality requirements. One is faster and cheaper for the company’s representative workload. What is the best next selection step?
options: Benchmark the tradeoffs and choose the workload-appropriate model
why: Representative testing lets the team compare quality, latency and cost against requirements.
reasons: Size alone does not show suitability once quality requirements are met.
Representative testing lets the team compare quality, latency and cost against requirements.
Popularity is not evidence that the model meets this workload’s constraints.
Measured latency and cost are directly relevant selection criteria.

clues.why: Evaluate the actual use case rather than a generic ranking.

hint: Look for a decision grounded in requirements and measured tradeoffs.
analysis: Both candidates pass the quality threshold. Compare cost and responsiveness under realistic conditions before choosing.
trap: The largest or most famous model is not automatically the best business fit.

q: A support assistant must use a changing product manual and follow a demonstrated response format. The team will keep the existing model weights and cannot fit the entire manual in one prompt. Which TWO approaches jointly meet the requirements?
options: Retrieve relevant manual passages for each request
Fine-tune on pairs of customer questions and approved replies
Include a few demonstrations of the required format in the prompt
Continue pre-training on the complete manual
Cache a successful response and reuse it for similar requests
reasons: Retrieval selects relevant passages from the manual within the available context; its index must be kept current.
Fine-tuning can adapt responses but updates model weights, violating the stated constraint.
Few-shot demonstrations guide the requested format at inference time without training.
Continued pre-training changes model weights and does not meet the no-training constraint.
Reused responses can contain stale or mismatched facts and do not jointly provide current evidence and format demonstrations.
why: Retrieval supplies relevant manual evidence at request time, while few-shot examples demonstrate the format. Neither approach changes the model’s weights.

clues.why: Eliminate training-based changes.
The facts must come from updated request-time context.

hint: One approach must supply relevant facts; the other must demonstrate the format without training.
analysis: Check both requirements together. Prompt examples show how to respond, while retrieval supplies what the current answer should be based on.
trap: Choosing two methods that address style but do not provide fresh product facts.
transfer: A lease assistant can retrieve the relevant contract section and use a few examples to produce a consistent summary format.

q: A model must label sentiment from an instruction with no demonstrations in the prompt. Which prompting technique is this?
why: Zero-shot asks the model to perform the task without demonstrations.
reasons: Few-shot includes a small set of demonstrations.
Zero-shot asks the model to perform the task without demonstrations.
Distillation trains a student from a teacher.
Continuous pre-training changes model parameters with additional training.

clues.why: Count examples rather than instructions.

hint: An instruction is not the same thing as a worked example.
analysis: The task and output can be specified in detail while still being zero-shot if no demonstrations are supplied.
trap: Zero-shot does not mean the prompt contains no guidance.

q: An application needs semantic search over internal documents. What should be compared to find related meaning?
why: Embedding-vector similarity can help compare meaning between queries and documents.
reasons: Exact filenames can miss semantically related material with different wording.
Encryption keys serve security needs and are not semantic feature vectors.
Embedding-vector similarity can help compare meaning between queries and documents.
Creation time describes recency, not semantic similarity.

clues.why: The goal is similarity of meaning, not exact filename matching.

hint: Choose a representation designed for comparing semantic features.
analysis: Meaning-based retrieval commonly compares query and content embeddings. Retrieval quality still depends on the model and indexing strategy.
trap: Semantic similarity is useful evidence of relevance, not a guarantee of factual accuracy.

q: Why might a RAG pipeline split long source documents into chunks?
options: To retrieve focused passages that fit the available context
why: Focused chunks can improve passage retrieval and fit within input constraints.
reasons: Chunking can preserve source metadata; hiding references is not its purpose.
Chunking alone cannot guarantee fairness or factual correctness.
Focused chunks can improve passage retrieval and fit within input constraints.
Access controls remain necessary regardless of chunk size.

clues.why: Retrieval needs manageable units within context limits.

hint: Think about what the retriever returns and the model can accept.
analysis: Chunking creates units suitable for retrieval and context assembly. Chunk size should preserve enough surrounding meaning for the task.
trap: Smaller chunks are not always better; too little context can break meaning.

q: A RAG chatbot cites a policy paragraph that was replaced last month. What should the team investigate first?
options: Check source freshness and index synchronization
Switch to a larger model without checking the retrieved context
why: Check source versions, ingestion and index updates to determine why obsolete information was retrieved.
reasons: Temperature changes sampling behavior and does not refresh outdated documents.
Check source versions, ingestion and index updates to determine why obsolete information was retrieved.
Longer output can still repeat the same obsolete passage.
A larger model can receive and rely on the same stale context; inspect retrieval first.

clues.why: The content used for grounding is outdated.

hint: Trace the answer back to the source and its ingestion process.
analysis: The visible failure is stale grounding material. Check source versions, refresh processes and retrieval results before changing the model.
trap: A citation proves a source was referenced, not that the source is current.

q: A prompt asks for a JSON object with three named fields. What most directly improves the chance of the desired format?
options: Describe only the topic and omit the field names
Specify the required schema and a valid example, then validate output
Use a higher temperature to encourage format variation
Repeat an ambiguous request several times without testing
why: Clear structure and a valid example improve guidance; programmatic validation still checks whether the response meets the contract.
reasons: Omitting field names leaves the required output structure ambiguous.
Clear structure and a valid example improve guidance; programmatic validation still checks whether the response meets the contract.
More variation does not directly improve adherence to an exact JSON structure.
Repeating ambiguity does not resolve it or verify valid JSON.

clues.why: The desired structure should be explicit.

hint: Choose the change that removes ambiguity from the requested output.
analysis: Specify fields, constraints and an example. Validate the response programmatically because prompting alone does not guarantee valid JSON.
trap: A well-written format instruction still needs output validation in production.

q: A model response must stop after a short answer. Which inference setting most directly limits generated length?
why: Maximum output tokens directly caps generation length, although a cap can truncate content.
reasons: Maximum output tokens directly caps generation length, although a cap can truncate content.
Temperature influences sampling variation, not a hard length cap.
Top P controls the candidate token distribution, not the maximum output length.
Examples can guide behavior but do not enforce a hard output-length limit.

clues.why: The control should act on output tokens.

hint: Separate inference settings from training and infrastructure settings.
analysis: The requirement is a length cap. Use the output-token limit and check that the resulting answer is complete enough.
trap: Truncating an answer is not the same as teaching the model to be concise.

q: Match each foundation-model evaluation technique to what it assesses.
reasons: BERTScore uses contextual embeddings to compare generated and reference text.
BLEU uses n-gram precision with a brevity penalty and is commonly associated with translation.
An LLM judge evaluates responses against supplied criteria but can have its own biases and errors.
ROUGE measures overlap with reference text and is commonly used for summaries.
why: BLEU is associated with translation overlap; ROUGE with summary overlap; BERTScore with semantic comparison; an LLM judge with rubric-based model assessment.

clues.why: Distinguish reference overlap, semantic similarity and model-based judgment.

hint: Identify how each metric compares or judges the generated response.
analysis: Different techniques capture different aspects of text quality. None of these alone guarantees factual correctness.
trap: A good overlap score does not prove truth; a model judge also needs validation.
prompts: Translation comparison using n-gram precision and a brevity penalty
A language model scores answers against a rubric

q: A summarization team wants an overlap-based metric comparing generated summaries with reference summaries. Which fits?
why: ROUGE compares overlap with reference text and is commonly used for summary evaluation.
reasons: ROUGE compares overlap with reference text and is commonly used for summary evaluation.
Latency measures response time, not overlap with a reference summary.
Task completion is a business outcome measure rather than a reference-overlap metric.
Throughput measures processing volume or speed, not textual summary overlap.

clues.why: A reference-text comparison is requested.

hint: Separate content-quality measures from system-operation measures.
analysis: The requirement is summary overlap, which points to ROUGE. Add checks for factuality because overlap alone does not establish truth.
trap: A summary can share many words with a reference and still contain factual errors.

q: A company uses another language model to score generated answers. What is an important evaluation risk?
options: The judge can have its own biases and errors
The candidate model no longer needs prompts
why: Model judges can be biased or mistaken; calibrate them against suitable criteria and human judgments.
reasons: Model judges can be biased or mistaken; calibrate them against suitable criteria and human judgments.
A second model is not an infallible source of truth.
Human review remains possible and can help validate the evaluation.
A judge does not eliminate the candidate model’s input requirements.

clues.why: The evaluator is itself a fallible model.

hint: Apply the same skepticism to the evaluator as to the system being evaluated.
analysis: LLM-as-a-judge can scale assessment but requires validation. Compare judgments against trusted examples and inspect disagreement.
trap: Automating an evaluation does not remove subjectivity or error.

q: A support agent retrieves correct documents but frequently fails to complete refund tasks. What should its evaluation include?
options: End-to-end task completion and tool outcomes
why: End-to-end testing captures whether the agent achieves the requested outcome with its tools.
reasons: Retrieval relevance alone misses planning or tool-execution failures.
Model size does not establish that the workflow completes successfully.
End-to-end testing captures whether the agent achieves the requested outcome with its tools.
Document count does not measure execution success.

clues.why: The failure occurs at the workflow outcome, not necessarily retrieval.

hint: Evaluate the whole application rather than only a good component.
analysis: Correct retrieval is necessary but insufficient for a tool-using agent. Assess completion, failures and safe handling of actions.
trap: A component score can be high while the user experience still fails.

q: A team repeatedly changes prompts and cannot tell which version caused a quality regression. What practice helps?
options: Version prompts and record evaluation results
why: Versioning and associated results allow changes and regressions to be traced.
reasons: Deleting history makes comparing behavior harder.
Versioning and associated results allow changes and regressions to be traced.
Hiding test data from the development process does not establish prompt history.
Length alone does not capture the relevant quality regression.

clues.why: The need is traceability of changes and their measured effects.

hint: Choose a practice that connects an artifact version with evidence.
analysis: Record prompt versions and run comparable evaluations for each change. Otherwise multiple changes can obscure the cause.
trap: More prompt experimentation is not helpful if changes and results are not tracked.

q: A chatbot must answer using private company documents and show the supporting source passages. Which Bedrock capability best fits?
why: Knowledge Bases supports retrieving connected source material for grounded responses and source references.
reasons: Knowledge Bases supports retrieving connected source material for grounded responses and source references.
Guardrails provides safeguards but does not itself replace document ingestion and retrieval.
Artifact provides AWS compliance documents, not a general question-answering store for the company’s private policies.
Comprehend analyzes text; it is not the Bedrock retrieval-and-grounded-generation capability.

clues.why: The answer must be grounded in the company’s own documents.

hint: Identify the retrieval-and-grounding requirement before selecting a service.
analysis: Use document retrieval and grounding rather than a speech service. Document access controls and source freshness still require attention.
trap: Do not confuse AWS compliance reports with a knowledge base over your own business documents.

q: A team wants one place to document a model’s intended use, limitations and evaluation results. What fits?
why: A Model Card records key model details, intended use, limitations and evaluation information.
reasons: An activity log does not replace structured documentation of intended use and limitations.
A Model Card records key model details, intended use, limitations and evaluation information.
IAM policies define permissions rather than documenting the model’s intended use.
A vector index supports retrieval rather than serving as a model governance record.

clues.why: The goal is transparent model documentation.

hint: Choose the artifact that explains the model to stakeholders.
analysis: The question asks for a model-information record. Documentation improves transparency but does not itself prove the model is fair or safe.
trap: A model card is evidence of documentation, not a certification of correctness.

q: A model will serve three regions. One region has very few examples in both training and evaluation data. Before claiming comparable regional performance, which TWO actions most directly address this evidence gap?
options: Evaluate each region with an adequately sized, suitable held-out sample
Increase the size of the existing majority-region evaluation sample
Curate appropriately sourced examples for the underrepresented region and reassess after model changes
Apply the same confidence threshold across regions without collecting additional evidence
Report a population-weighted average of the existing regional scores
reasons: Adequate, suitable regional samples support meaningful comparisons without using training outcomes as proof.
More examples from the already well-represented region do not fill the missing region’s evidence gap.
Relevant representative data can address the coverage gap; separate evaluation must test the resulting model.
A shared threshold does not supply missing data or establish comparable performance.
A weighted average can hide poor performance in a small region and leaves the evidence gap unresolved.
why: Suitable held-out evaluation measures regional outcomes, and representative data addresses the coverage gap. Reassess all regions after changes.

clues.why: The gap affects learning and the evidence used to assess it.

hint: Choose a measurement step and a representation step that address the missing region.
analysis: Both training coverage and evaluation evidence are limited. Improve representation where appropriate, keep evaluation independent and check for new disparities after changes.
trap: Treating a large total dataset or a strong weighted average as proof of regional performance.
transfer: Adding more English examples does not establish reliable performance for a language missing from the test set.

q: A team selects an AI model for routine tasks that a smaller model can handle at the required quality. Which choice supports sustainability?
options: Consider a smaller suitable model and measure resource use
Run redundant inference without a need
why: Choosing a fit-for-purpose model and measuring resource use can reduce unnecessary computation.
reasons: A larger model can consume unnecessary resources when the smaller one meets the task.
Choosing a fit-for-purpose model and measuring resource use can reduce unnecessary computation.
Unneeded output can increase compute and cost.
Unnecessary repeated inference adds work without a justified benefit.

clues.why: The smaller model already meets the business threshold.

hint: Balance adequate quality against resource consumption.
analysis: The task does not need the largest model. Evaluate a smaller suitable model rather than assuming more computation is always better.
trap: Sustainability should not be claimed from size alone; measure the relevant workload.

q: A user needs to challenge an AI-assisted decision that affects them. Which design best supports accountability?
options: Provide no explanation or appeal route
Offer understandable reasons and a human review channel
Treat the model’s confidence as final authority
why: Understandable reasons and human review support accountability and correction.
reasons: Without explanation or review, a user cannot meaningfully contest a possible error.
Understandable reasons and human review support accountability and correction.
Confidence is not a guarantee that a decision is appropriate.
Blocking feedback prevents problems being raised and investigated.

clues.why: Users need a way to understand and contest the outcome.

hint: Think about the person affected, not just the automated workflow.
analysis: An accountable system gives understandable information and a path to review. The design should reflect the impact of the decision.
trap: A technical explanation alone may be insufficient if no correction process exists.

q: Which AWS service helps assess resource configurations against defined rules over time?
why: Config records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules.
reasons: Config records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules.
CloudTrail records supported API activity; that differs from evaluating configuration state against a rule.
Metrics monitor operational quantities rather than replacing resource configuration compliance checks.
Artifact supplies compliance documents rather than tracking your resource configurations over time.

clues.why: The requirement is configuration compliance rather than API event history.

hint: Distinguish resource state from records of who called an API.
analysis: The focus is whether configured resources comply with rules. CloudTrail would address account API activity, a related but different question.
trap: Audit and compliance tools overlap in purpose but capture different evidence.

q: A team needs AWS compliance reports and agreements to support a review. Which service provides access to these documents?
why: Artifact provides access to AWS compliance reports and agreements.
reasons: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 rather than providing AWS compliance reports.
Transcribe handles speech-to-text conversion.
Artifact provides access to AWS compliance reports and agreements.
Knowledge Bases retrieves connected business data; it is not the primary AWS compliance-report portal.

clues.why: The company needs AWS-provided documentation.

hint: Ask whether the task is obtaining reports or scanning the company’s data.
analysis: The required evidence is AWS compliance documentation, which differs from monitoring a customer’s resources.
trap: Accessing a compliance report does not automatically make your application compliant.

q: A model accesses customer data through a managed AWS service. Which statement best reflects shared responsibility?
options: AWS handles every customer data decision
The customer still controls appropriate permissions and data handling
The customer must own all AWS physical servers
why: Customer responsibilities include appropriate data handling and access controls; exact duties vary by service.
reasons: The customer retains responsibilities for its data and access choices.
Customer responsibilities include appropriate data handling and access controls; exact duties vary by service.
Encryption remains relevant for managed services.
AWS operates its physical infrastructure; customer ownership of it is not required.

clues.why: Management shifts some duties but does not eliminate customer obligations.

hint: Reject both extremes: no customer responsibility and all infrastructure responsibility.
analysis: Apply the service-specific shared responsibility model. Data and access decisions do not disappear just because a service is managed.
trap: The division of duties varies by service and configuration.

q: An order assistant may read order status but must not issue refunds. Even if an injected instruction makes the model request a refund, which TWO controls independently restrict what can execute?
options: Use a runtime identity whose downstream permissions allow only order lookup
Put the no-refund rule in the system prompt and inspect its wording during testing
Authorize each tool call at the execution boundary against an approved read-only action set
Record refund attempts in an audit log and review them after execution
Require a high model-confidence score before executing a refund request
reasons: The actual credential must lack refund capability; hiding a tool while retaining broad credentials is insufficient.
Prompt instructions guide behavior but cannot serve as the permission boundary if the model requests a forbidden action.
The execution layer rejects operations outside the approved read-only set before any side effect occurs.
Logging helps detection and investigation but does not prevent the prohibited refund.
A confident unsafe request is still unsafe; a confidence threshold does not authorize an action.
why: Least-privilege downstream permissions and execution-time authorization enforce the action boundary even when the model generates an unsafe request.

clues.why: The controls must block the action outside the model’s text decision.

hint: Distinguish prevention before a side effect from model guidance and after-the-fact detection.
analysis: Trace the request through to the credential and API that would perform it. Both identity permissions and tool authorization must restrict the actual action path.
trap: Confusing an instruction, an audit record or model confidence with an enforceable permission.
concept: Least privilege and agent action boundaries
transfer: A reporting assistant needs read-only access to accounting data even if its prompt says never to edit records.
